Wheat blast on wheat in Brazil

Source: vignettes/case-study-brazil-wheat-blast.Rmd
case-study-brazil-wheat-blast.Rmd

🎯 Goal

This vignette demonstrates how to use FraNchEstYN to estimate wheat yield losses from wheat head blast in Brazil.

The workflow follows three progressive steps:

  1. Calibration: fit crop and disease parameters on a subset of planting periods (1, 5 and 10).
  2. Parameter averaging: derive robust mean crop and disease parameters across planting periods.
  3. Validation: apply the averaged parameters to all planting periods, and compare simulated vs observed disease severity and yield.

We start from the Brazil wheat parameter set bundled with the package (cropParameters_brazil), and use open-access EPAMIG experimental data (dos Santos et al., 2023; 12 sowing dates × 6 years for cultivar BRILHANTE) with daily weather from NASA POWER.

📦 Packages

We load FraNchEstYN plus helper libraries for wrangling, visualization, and reproducible tables.

library(FraNchEstYN)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(scales)
library(kableExtra)

📥 Data loading

We use three sources:

  • weather_data: daily NASA POWER weather for Empresa de Pesquisa Agropecuária de Minas Gerais (EPAMIG) in the municipality of Patos de Minas, in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil (18°31′04.0”S, 46°26′25.0”W)
  • management_data: basic agronomic metadata (crop, sowing DOY, etc.)
  • reference_data: measured yields and disease severity for one cultivar (BRILHANTE), six years and 12 sowing dates

We rely on NASAPOWER package (maintained by Adam Sparks 🙏) to directly query daily weather data.

🛰 NASA Power data

We request maximum and minimum temperature and precipitation from 2011–2020. Data are tagged with location and date components to simplify later filtering.

# --- Load libraries
library(nasapower)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# --- Retrieve daily data from NASA POWER
weather_data <- nasapower::get_power(
  community     = "ag",
  lonlat        = c(-46.4403, -18.5178),
  dates         = c("2011-01-01", "2020-12-31"),
  temporal_api  = "daily",
  pars          = c("T2M_MAX", "T2M_MIN", "PRECTOTCORR")
) %>%
  rename(
    TMAX = T2M_MAX,
    TMIN = T2M_MIN,
    RAIN = PRECTOTCORR,
    DATE = YYYYMMDD
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    year  = year(DATE),
    month = month(DATE),
    day   = day(DATE),
    Site  = "Sertaozinho",
    lat   = -18.5178
  ) %>%
  select(Site, TMAX, TMIN, RAIN, year, month, day, lat)

📑 Management and reference datasets

For convenience, the package already includes the management and reference datasets, derived from the open-access EPAMIG wheat trials (cultivar BRILHANTE, multiple sowing dates and years). The original experiments are described in dos Santos et al. (2023).

# comes with the package
data("reference_brazil")
data("management_brazil")

# a single cultivar (BRILHANTE) is simulated: label it "Generic" so that
# management, reference and crop parameters refer to the same variety
reference_brazil  <- reference_brazil  |> mutate(variety = "Generic")
management_brazil <- management_brazil |> mutate(variety = "Generic",
                                                 site    = "Sertaozinho")

🦠 Step 1 — Crop and disease calibration on selected sowing dates

As in the published analysis, crop and disease parameters are calibrated together (calibration = "all") on three sowing dates, and the remaining sowing dates are kept for validation.

👉 The idea is:

  • Select a subset of sowing dates (planting periods 1, 5 and 10, as in the article) for calibration.
  • For the crop, calibrate only cycle length, flowering start and radiation use efficiency.
  • For wheat blast, start from the default parameters with the same settings used in the article.
  • Run franchestyn separately for each planting period.
  • Collect the estimated crop and disease parameters from each run.
  • Average them across planting periods and rebuild consistent parameter sets.
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 📌 Step 1: Crop + disease calibration on selected sowing dates
# --------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Load the Brazil wheat parameter set bundled with the package
data("cropParameters_brazil")

# 2. Crop: calibrate only phenology and radiation use efficiency
thisCropParam <- FraNchEstYN::disable_all_calibration(cropParameters_brazil)
thisCropParam$CycleLength$calibration            <- TRUE
thisCropParam$CycleLength$min                    <- 1500
thisCropParam$CycleLength$max                    <- 2500
thisCropParam$RadiationUseEfficiency$calibration <- TRUE
thisCropParam$FloweringStart$calibration         <- TRUE

# 3. Disease: default wheat blast parameters, with the settings used in the article
thisDiseaseParam <- diseaseParameters$wheat_blast
thisDiseaseParam$SenescenceAcceleratorDamage$calibration <- FALSE
thisDiseaseParam$SenescenceAcceleratorDamage$value       <- 0
thisDiseaseParam$SenescenceAcceleratorDamage$max         <- 0.5
thisDiseaseParam$LightStealerDamage$calibration          <- FALSE
thisDiseaseParam$LightStealerDamage$value                <- 0
thisDiseaseParam$AssimilateSappersDamage$value           <- 0
thisDiseaseParam$AssimilateSappersDamage$calibration     <- TRUE
thisDiseaseParam$CyclePercentageOnset$min                <- 20
thisDiseaseParam$OuterInoculumShapeRelease$value         <- 1
thisDiseaseParam$OuterInoculumShapeParameter$value       <- 0
thisDiseaseParam$IsSplashBorne$value                     <- 0

# 4. Study period and calibration sowing dates
start_end <- c(2011, 2020)
pps <- c(1, 5, 10)

all_parameters_crop    <- list()
all_parameters_disease <- list()

# 5. Calibrate on each planting period
for (pp in pps) {

  df <- FraNchEstYN::franchestyn(
    weather_data      = weather_data,
    management_data   = management_brazil |> filter(planting_period == pp),
    reference_data    = reference_brazil  |> filter(planting_period == pp),
    cropParameters    = thisCropParam,
    diseaseParameters = thisDiseaseParam,
    calibration       = "all",     # crop + disease
    start_end         = start_end,
    iterations        = 999        # simplex iterations
  )

  all_parameters_crop[[length(all_parameters_crop) + 1]] <-
    parameters_to_df(df$parameters$crop) |> mutate(planting_period = pp)
  all_parameters_disease[[length(all_parameters_disease) + 1]] <-
    parameters_to_df(df$parameters$disease) |> mutate(planting_period = pp)
}

# 6. Merge the calibrations from all planting periods
parameters_df_crop <- dplyr::bind_rows(all_parameters_crop,    .id = "run_id")
parameters_df      <- dplyr::bind_rows(all_parameters_disease, .id = "run_id")

We then average across planting periods:

# 7. Mean, standard deviation and sample size across planting periods
summarise_params <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    group_by(Parameter) %>%
    summarise(
      value    = mean(as.numeric(Value), na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_value = sd(as.numeric(Value),   na.rm = TRUE),
      n        = sum(!is.na(Value)),
      .groups  = "drop"
    )
}
param_summary_crop <- summarise_params(parameters_df_crop)
param_summary      <- summarise_params(parameters_df)

# 8. Rebuild parameter lists with the averaged values (±20% range)
#    and switch calibration off for the validation runs
calibCrop    <- FraNchEstYN::df_to_parameters(param_summary_crop, range_pct = 0.2) |>
  FraNchEstYN::disable_all_calibration()
calibDisease <- FraNchEstYN::df_to_parameters(param_summary, range_pct = 0.2) |>
  FraNchEstYN::disable_all_calibration()

At this stage, calibCrop and calibDisease contain the crop and epidemiological parameters averaged across the calibration sowing dates. This reduces noise from single calibrations and provides a robust baseline for validation on the remaining experiments.

🌾 Step 2 — Batch validation

We validate the averaged parameters across all sowing periods and years.

The procedure is straightforward:

  1. Loop across planting periods recorded in the dataset.
  2. Run FraNchEstYN without further calibration, using the averaged crop and disease parameters (calibCrop, calibDisease).
  3. Collect simulation outputs for each planting period.
  4. Bind everything into one tibble for further analysis and plotting.

📊 Step 3 — Validation against experiments

In this final step we bring together the model simulations and the field observations from EPAMIG.
We join the simulated outputs with the observed disease severity (DisSev) and yield per planting period, making sure that only the last record of each experimental group retains observed values (all intermediate time steps are set to NA).

🎨 Visualization

To compare simulations with experiments, we rescale yield onto the same axis (by dividing by a scaling factor) and facet the plot by year × planting experiment.

The final plot shows:

  • Healthy light interception (green area)
  • Simulated light interception (dark green line)
  • Disease severity (blue line and points)
  • Grain yield (black line and points, rescaled)

🌍 Interpretation and conclusion

The plot above summarizes model simulations against observed data for six years and twelve sowing dates of cultivar BRILHANTE in Brazil.

  • ✅ Healthy light interception (green area) provides the baseline without disease.
  • ✅ Simulated interception (dark green line) captures crop canopy dynamics.
  • ✅ Disease severity (blue) is both simulated (line) and observed (points).
  • ✅ Yield (black) shows observed vs simulated grain yield (scaled to fit).

Overall, the calibrated disease parameters reproduce the magnitude and seasonal patterns of wheat blast epidemics. The framework highlights how integrating weather, management, and epidemiology can provide robust estimates of yield losses.

📌 Key takeaway

This vignette illustrated the full calibration–validation cycle:

  1. Calibrate crop and disease parameters on a subset of experiments.
  2. Average them into a robust epidemiological baseline.
  3. Validate on all experiments across years and sowing dates; the nine sowing dates not used for calibration provide the independent test.

This workflow can be extended to other crops, pathosystems, and datasets using the same FraNchEstYN framework.
